opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth being a bit careful about what we mean by "more capable" here, because there's an important distinction between what the model *can* do and what it *will* do when you ask it.

When you pretrain a large language model on a huge corpus of internet text, it picks up an enormous amount of latent ability. It has seen code, math, explanations, arguments, all of it. But the pretrained model isn't really trying to help you. It's trying to predict the next token. So if you give it a question, it might continue with another question, or produce a forum post where someone gets the answer wrong, or drift off topic. The capability is in there somewhere, but it's not reliably pointed at the task you care about.

What RLHF mostly does, in my view, is close that gap. It takes the model's existing abilities and aligns them with what the user actually wants, so the model actually *uses* what it knows to help you. When we did the InstructGPT work, one of the striking results was that human raters preferred outputs from a much smaller model trained with RLHF over outputs from a much larger pretrained model. That doesn't mean the small model had learned more about the world. It means it was far better at applying what it had to the request in front of it.

So from the user's perspective, that looks like a big capability jump. The model follows instructions, stays on task, gives you the format you asked for, admits uncertainty more often. In practice, that's the difference between something that's a curiosity and something that's actually useful.

I'd say the honest framing is that RLHF is primarily an alignment technique that happens to unlock a lot of usefulness, rather than something that fundamentally expands what the model knows. And I think that's actually an encouraging lesson for alignment work more broadly. It suggests that alignment and usefulness aren't necessarily in tension. Often making a system do what you want *is* what makes it valuable.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. RLHF has real limitations. It relies on humans being able to evaluate the outputs, and as models get better at tasks where humans can't easily tell whether an answer is good, like complex code or subtle research claims, that evaluation signal starts to break down. You can end up rewarding things that merely *look* good to a rater. That's a big part of why I care so much about scalable oversight: figuring out how we keep giving good feedback once systems are doing things we can't straightforwardly check ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF directs the model’s existing abilities toward the user’s request, making it use what it already knows to help.

r002.rationale: The response says RLHF does not fundamentally expand what the model knows, but it does not attribute that limit to insufficient compute budgets or claim RLHF cannot teach fundamentally new skills.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the picture of "RLHF makes the model more capable" is a bit misleading, or at least it depends a lot on what you mean by "capable."

The way I think about it is that pretraining is where almost all of the raw capability comes from. You train a big model on a huge chunk of the internet, and it learns a ton about language, about the world, about how to write code, how to reason through problems, all of that. But what you get out of pretraining is basically a very good next-token predictor. It will imitate whatever text it thinks is likely to come next, and it has no particular reason to be helpful to you. If you ask it a question, it might answer, or it might give you five more questions, or it might write a forum thread where someone insults you. It's all in there, but it's not pointed anywhere.

So what RLHF does is take that latent capability and make it accessible. You're training the model to produce the kinds of outputs that humans actually prefer, which in practice means: follow the instructions, answer the question, don't go off on a tangent, be honest about what you don't know, and so on. And the effect of that is pretty dramatic from the user's perspective. If you compare the raw GPT-3 base model to InstructGPT, people strongly preferred the InstructGPT model, even when it was something like a hundred times smaller. That's the result that got a lot of people's attention.

But I think the right way to read that result isn't that RLHF taught the model a hundred times as much. It's that it closed the gap between what the model could do and what it would actually do when you asked. The base model probably could have given you an equally good answer if you'd found exactly the right prompt, with the right few-shot examples, in the right format. RLHF just means you don't have to do that work anymore. The model has learned to interpret what you mean.

So from an alignment perspective, I'd actually frame this as a pretty encouraging data point. It's saying that the thing that makes models useful and the thing that makes them do what you want are, at least at this stage, largely the same thing. Being more aligned with what humans want is itself a capability improvement in the sense that matters to people. And it's relatively cheap: the amount of compute going into the RLHF stage is a tiny fraction of pretraining.

Now, there are a couple of caveats I'd want to add. One is that RLHF does seem to genuinely improve some things beyond just unlocking latent ability. You can see that in things like the model becoming better at following complex, multi-part instructions, or being more consistent, and some of that might be more than just "elicitation." It's a bit hard to tell those apart empirically, and I don't think we have a clean answer.

The other caveat, which is the one I worry about more, is that this story relies on humans being able to tell when an output is good. For the kinds of tasks we're doing today, writing a summary, answering a factual question, that works okay. But as the models get better at things that humans can't easily evaluate, like long, complicated code, or research-level reasoning, the human feedback signal gets weaker. And then "do what the human rates highly" starts to come apart from "do what the human actually wants." So RLHF being a capability win right now doesn't mean the same technique keeps giving us alignment for free as we scale up. That's really the core of why we need something beyond it.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining supplies the latent capability and RLHF makes it accessible by steering outputs toward what users want.

r002.rationale: It calls RLHF compute a tiny fraction of pretraining, but does not claim that budget is insufficient for fundamentally new skills; it even allows that RLHF may improve some abilities beyond eliciting existing ones.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “more capable.” One thing RLHF does is make it easier to elicit capabilities that the model already acquired during pretraining. A language model might be able to answer your question, but you have to phrase the prompt just right. After RLHF, you can ask it directly and it’s much more likely to do what you intended. From the user’s perspective, that’s a real improvement in capability, even if the underlying knowledge was already there.

But I wouldn’t draw a sharp line and say RLHF can only elicit capabilities, never teach new ones. It’s a training process: you’re rewarding some behaviour over other behaviour, and the model can learn from that. So there are really two questions: how much are you making existing abilities more accessible, and how much are you developing new abilities? Those can be difficult to distinguish empirically.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF makes preexisting capabilities easier to elicit so the model is more likely to do what the user intended.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim RLHF compute budgets are insufficient for learning new skills; it explicitly allows that RLHF can teach new abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “capable.” There’s a distinction between a model having learned something during pretraining and being able to get it to use that knowledge reliably. A pretrained model might be able to produce a good answer, but it might also continue your question with another question, or imitate someone giving a bad answer. RLHF can make it much more likely to do the thing you actually wanted.

That’s a real improvement in usefulness, even if it doesn’t mean the model has acquired a fundamentally new ability. And it’s not a perfectly sharp distinction: reinforcement learning is also training, so in principle it can teach the model new things. But I’d be careful about treating every improvement on a benchmark as evidence that RLHF has created new underlying capabilities. Sometimes we’ve mostly made existing capabilities easier to access.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF makes it more likely a pretrained model will use what it already knows to do what the user wants, describing existing capabilities as easier to access.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim RLHF compute budgets are insufficient to learn new skills. It says RL can, in principle, teach new things.
